title: Optimize Console: prefetch & batching savings playbook sprint — Obsidian Logistics
summary: Redwood ran an Optimize Console walkthrough focused on prefetch (prefix/KV) and batching levers for an LLM-driven logistics assistant. Discussed current traffic profile, sessionization, expected latency budget, VPC requirements, SOC2/KMS concerns, and a savings simulation. Agreed to run a small sandbox with a 2-week traffic replay and deliver a cost-savings snapshot + runbook.
next_steps: Redwood: provision savings sandbox and share replay instructions
Redwood: deliver cost-savings snapshot and playbook within 7 business days

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-05-20 16:00 PT
Duration: ~58 minutes
Attendees: Hannah Lee (Redwood AE), Carlos Rivera (Redwood SE), Priya Nair (Redwood CSM) — Maya Chen (Head of ML, Obsidian), Raj Patel (Platform Eng), Sofia Martinez (CTO)

Auto-summary:
- Quick recap of Obsidian's use case: an LLM assistant that manages routing/warehouse Q&A and generates manifests. High throughput during 2x daily dispatch windows; many short sessions with repeated prefixes (tracking IDs, order history)
- Primary ask: reduce token/unit cost without degrading 99th pct latency under 250ms for the interactive UI

Topics covered: prefetch/prefix KV, batching strategy, sessionization, cost sim, security/VPC considerations

[00:00] Hannah (Redwood): hey everyone, thanks for joining, we thought we'd run through an Optimize Console sprint — the idea is pragmatic prefetch + batching levers tied to a cost sim. quick intros?

[00:18] Maya (Obsidian): maya here — i'm head of ml at obsidian, we run the assistant in prod for our dispatcher ui, big spikes at 6am and 6pm, lots of short lived sessions, a lot of repeated prefixes — order id, carrier info, standard Qs

[00:32] Carlos (Redwood): awesome, thanks. i'm carlos, i'll lead the technical bit — first slide is a cost profile we sent earlier — does that align with your telemetry?

[00:45] Raj (Obsidian): yeah mostly. our 50th pct latency's fine but the tail is where we get complaints — especially when we hit the dispatch spike. curious what prefetch actually buys us versus larger batch windows

[01:05] Carlos: uh-huh. short answer: prefix/KV prefetch reduces per-request generation tokens by reusing cached KV and can keep latency low if keys are well scoped. batching reduces per-token GPU overhead but increases serialization latency unless you set concurrency and max-wait properly

[01:28] Hannah: we'll demo two lanes: a conservative prefetch (session-scoped prefixes only) and an aggressive lookahead that attempts KV for repeated customer patterns. we'll run sims against your sample trace in the sandbox

[02:05] Sofia (Obsidian): quick compliance note — we need to keep everything inside our VPC for now, and KMS-hsm for keys. does dedicated vs hosted change prefetch behavior?

[02:20] Priya (Redwood): good question — functionally the prefetch/cache behavior is the same across Hosted/Dedicated/Private, but dedicated/private gives you control for data residency and KMS. we can do the sandbox in a private cluster vpc-peered to your environment for testing

[02:48] Maya: ok great. also curious on eviction TTLs — some of our prefixes are only hot for 20 minutes between two runs. what's the rule of thumb?

[03:04] Carlos: TTL is workload specific — best practice we showed: align prefix TTL to session heat windows; e.g., set short TTLs for per-dispatch prefixes, longer for account-wide conversational memory. we usually recommend a tiered TTL with a hot set and warm set

[03:28] Raj: and how does that interact with batching? if we keep small TTLs to keep cache relevant, do we lose batching opportunities?

[03:40] Carlos: they interact — prefetch increases cache hits, which can reduce tokens and thus make batching yield less absolute token savings but still improves throughput because cached KVs are faster to rehydrate than regenerating. there is a sweet spot — our Optimize console sim helps find it by replaying traces with varying TTL/batch windows

[04:10] Hannah: switching to the cost sim — here's an example scenario: baseline hosted model (gpt-variant-open) at x tokens, baseline unit cost y. if you enable conservative prefetch and 8-concurrency batching, you see ~28% token reduction in this trace and marginal latency changes. aggressive lookahead with 16-concurrency reduces tokens ~42% but tail latency bumps — see the 95/99 numbers

[04:45] Maya: that's useful — what does 'aggressive lookahead' actually do? is it speculative decode?

[04:58] Carlos: not speculative decode, more like predicted KV keys derived from session patterns — we attempt a key lookup for likely next prefixes. if miss, we fall back. fallback is important: you don't want more latency from repeated misses. we set a quick timeout for KV lookups and run them in parallel to avoid serialization overhead

[05:28] Sofia: are we safe from data leakage if we prefetch predicted keys? we share some customer-sensitive identifiers

[05:40] Priya: we recommend hashing prefixes and storing with customer-scoped namespaces; access controls via RBAC and KMS encryption at rest. Redwood's private deployment supports your KMS/HSM flow and audit logs for each KV access

[06:05] Raj: can we see an example of the console? you mentioned the sandbox will let us replay our traffic and toggle TTLs

[06:15] Carlos: yep — i'll share my screen and step through the Optimize console. (screen share noise) here is the trace replay UI, you can upload a gzipped sample, set model variant, concurrency, max-wait-ms, and prefix TTL buckets

[06:40] [screen noise / some overlap] Carlos: on the right is the cost delta chart, token breakdown by generation vs lookup, and latency distribution. we can export a CSV for your finance team. also link to the runbook in chat — redwood.com/sandbox/runbook (note: placeholder link, we will share the real one)

[07:12] Maya: looks neat. one of our constraints: our UI expects <250ms 99th for interactive autocomplete during manual edits. can you simulate 99th with network overhead?

[07:26] Carlos: console lets you add synthetic network latency; we typically add your reported network RTT and a jitter model. in the sandbox we'll use your sample RTT numbers and approximate retries

[07:50] Raj: question on quotas and throttles — if we run aggressive batching, does Redwood queue requests and cause head-of-line blocking?

[08:05] Hannah: no, we have request routing and concurrency controls — you can set per-route concurrency and fallback routing to a faster variant or dedicated pool. the console demo includes retry and fallback policy configs

[08:30] Sofia: we also want to know what success looks like — for procurement we need a clear cost reduction estimate and an ops runbook for rollouts

[08:42] Hannah: agreed — our deliverable will be: 1) a cost-savings snapshot with sensitivity ranges; 2) a step-by-step playbook for TTLs and batching config; 3) a plan for a 2-week sandbox run with checkpoints

[09:05] Carlos: i'd like to highlight a micro-optimization we often see: session affinity. if you attach sessions to a warm KV shard, you'll get much higher hit rates than random routing. the tradeoff is slightly uneven load distribution — we can simulate both

[09:28] Maya: do you have any guardrails for the affinity? we don't want long-lived shards that cause hot GPU exhaustion

[09:40] Carlos: yes — we recommend shard TTLs and automatic shard draining when load exceeds a threshold; the console has a shard health dashboard and you can set autoscale triggers for burst capacity

[10:05] Raj: what about model quantization — can we run smaller quantized variants for cheaper tokens and still keep latency?

[10:18] Carlos: quantization is in the Optimize recommendations — for your average sequence length and our profile, int8 variants gave good cost reduction with minor quality delta; Optimize will flag quality regressions tied to your eval set. we always surface model-quality metrics alongside token savings

[10:45] Sofia: procurement will want to see SOC2 and audit evidence — can you share security docs and a pointer to the compliance package?

[10:56] Priya: yes we'll share the SOC2 report, ISO artifact list and the Private deployment compliance checklist. also if you want, we can sign an NDA before we exchange more sample data

[11:15] Maya: great — on the sandbox: does Redwood need full PII data? we prefer to mask or hash copies

[11:24] Hannah: that's standard — provide anonymized or hashed payloads, we support hashing and we can work with you on a minimal schema needed for useful simulations

[11:44] Carlos: i'd like to show a quick sim: baseline vs conservative prefetch vs aggressive prefetch with 3 TTL tiers. (running sim) baseline avg cost = $X per 1k requests, conservative saves ~26%, aggressive saves ~41% but 99th latency increases from 210ms to 310ms in this configuration

[12:20] Raj: ok that helps quantify the tradeoff. what's the recommended rollout path?

[12:28] Hannah: start conservative in a canary: session-scoped prefixes + short TTLs for dispatch windows, monitor hit-rate and 99th latency for 48-72h, then progressively enable lookahead in low-risk routes. we also recommend automated rollback if 99th exceeds your SLO

[13:00] Sofia: approximate effort to run this sandbox and the data we need?

[13:09] Priya: effort: Redwood will provision sandbox and give an upload spec. We'll need 48h gzipped traces (anonymized), SLOs, and a list of priority routes. Typical turnaround for the snapshot is 5-7 business days after data receipt

[13:28] Maya: sounds doable. any pitfalls we should watch out for?

[13:33] Carlos: one common pitfall — overly aggressive TTLs combined with affinity can create hot shards. second pitfall: lookahead mispredictions causing extra KV lookups if not bounded by quick timeouts

[13:50] Raj: thanks — one more: do you have a pricing model for the sandbox or is it included?

[13:58] Hannah: sandbox is included as part of the evaluation; long-term we'll discuss commit tiers if you move to Dedicated or Private. we'll include a pro-forma savings estimate that you can use in procurement decks

[14:20] Sofia: okay let's recap next steps quickly

[14:25] Hannah: recap: Maya will send sample traces by May 24; Redwood to provision sandbox and send upload instructions by May 27; Redwood to deliver cost-savings snapshot and initial playbook by May 28. action owners and due dates are in the chat notes. we'll also share SOC2 and compliance docs in parallel

[14:45] Maya: ok, thanks everyone — appreciate the practical demo. excited to see what we can save without breaking latency

[14:55] Hannah: great, we'll follow up with calendar invites for the sandbox kickoff and a link to the runbook. thanks all

[15:05] (call ends)

Notes on transcript: occasional speaker misattribs, some words garbled by background noise; placeholders used for links.
